questions.stem: After the April 2020 PSU bank merger, how many Public Sector Banks remain in India?
questions.explanation: Post April 2020 mega-merger, India has 12 Public Sector Banks (PSBs): (1) SBI, (2) PNB, (3) BoB, (4) Canara, (5) Union Bank of India, (6) Indian Bank, (7) Bank of India, (8) Bank of Maharashtra, (9) Central Bank of India, (10) Indian Overseas Bank, (11) Punjab & Sind Bank, (12) UCO Bank. The April 2020 round merged: PNB+OBC+United → PNB; Canara+Syndicate → Canara; Union+Andhra+Corp → Union; Indian+Allahabad → Indian. Earlier consolidations: SBI+5 associates+BMB (2017), BoB+Vijaya+Dena (2019).

questions.stem: A loan account is classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) in India if interest or principal remains overdue for more than:
questions.explanation: Per RBI's Prudential Norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning (IRAC), an account becomes NPA if interest/principal remains overdue for MORE THAN 90 DAYS for term loans (was 180 days before 2004; aligned with international norms). For agricultural loans, 2 crop seasons for short-duration crops / 1 for long-duration. Sub-categories: Sub-standard (NPA up to 12 months), Doubtful (NPA > 12 months), Loss asset (unrecoverable). Recognised GROSS NPA minus provisions = NET NPA. Total NPAs fell from 11.2% in 2018 to ~2.6% in 2024 (lowest in a decade).

questions.stem: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) was enacted in which year and what is the target resolution period?
questions.explanation: IBC 2016 (effective 28 May 2016) unified India's bankruptcy laws. Under Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP): 180-day initial period + one-time 90-day extension = MAX 270 days (extended to 330 days by 2019 amendment, including litigation time). Key institutions: IBBI (regulator), NCLT (adjudicating authority for corporates), NCLAT (appellate), IPAs (Insolvency Professional Agencies), Information Utilities. Notable cases: Essar Steel (resolved), Bhushan Steel (Tata took over), DHFL (Piramal bought). total 270 days.

questions.stem: Under Basel III norms implemented in India, what is the minimum Capital Adequacy Ratio (CRAR) required for a Scheduled Commercial Bank (SCB)?
questions.explanation: Basel III (global regulatory framework, implemented in India from 2013 onwards by RBI) prescribes MINIMUM CAR/CRAR = 9% for SCBs (higher than Basel's own 8% — India applied a stricter buffer). Additional requirement: Capital Conservation Buffer of 2.5% (so effective minimum 11.5%) + Counter-Cyclical Capital Buffer 0-2.5%. Tier 1 + Tier 2 capital / Risk Weighted Assets. For SFBs: 15% (with Tier 1 ≥ 7.5%). For UCBs: 9% (Tier 1) + 12% (Total, for Tier-2/3/4).

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a Small Finance Bank (SFB) in India?
questions.explanation: Bandhan Bank was initially an NBFC-MFI, became a UNIVERSAL COMMERCIAL BANK (not an SFB) when it received a banking license in 2015 — technically a Private Sector Bank. The 10 SFBs in India (original 10 licensees, 2015): AU, Capital, Equitas, ESAF, Fincare, Jana, North East, Suryoday, Ujjivan, Utkarsh. Shivalik Small Finance Bank became the 11th when it transitioned in 2021. Unity Small Finance Bank became the 12th (acquired PMC Bank in 2022). SFBs must lend 75% to priority sector (vs 40% for commercial banks) and 50% loans must be ≤ ₹25 lakh.

questions.stem: The SARFAESI Act, 2002, empowers banks to recover bad loans WITHOUT court intervention. What does SARFAESI stand for?

options.option_text: Securities and Reconstruction of Financial Assets & Enforcement of Security Interest
State Audit and Recovery Finance Act for Enforcement of Secured Instruments
Secured Assets Recovery and Financial Enforcement of Special Instruments
Scheduled Accounts Recovery by Financial Establishments & Secured Interest

questions.explanation: SARFAESI = Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002. Allows banks/FIs to: (1) securitise assets; (2) set up Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs); (3) enforce security interest WITHOUT court intervention — attach and sell defaulter's mortgaged assets after 60-day notice. Applies to loans above ₹1 lakh (now ₹20 lakh by 2021 amendment). Not applicable to: agricultural land, loans ≤ ₹1 lakh, and where 80% of loan is repaid. Critical tool alongside IBC 2016 for NPA resolution.

questions.stem: The Narasimham Committee (I, 1991), whose recommendations reshaped Indian banking in the 1990s, was headed by:
questions.explanation: M. Narasimham (1927-2021) — 13th RBI Governor (1977) and later Finance Secretary — chaired: (1) Narasimham Committee I (1991, post-BoP crisis) → recommended reducing SLR to 25%, CRR to 3-8%, phased interest rate deregulation, ending 'directed credit', prudential NPA norms, and phased banking deregulation; (2) Narasimham Committee II (1998) → further reforms: mergers of strong banks, restructured boards, asset reconstruction, Basel II. He is called the 'Father of Indian Banking Reforms'. 'Father of Economic Reforms' is Manmohan Singh as FM 1991-96.

questions.stem: Which Indian bank was the first to be established and is considered the oldest surviving bank?

options.option_text: State Bank of India via its predecessor Bank of Calcutta (1806)

questions.explanation: SBI's family tree: Bank of Calcutta (2 June 1806) → renamed Bank of Bengal (1809) → merged with Bank of Bombay (1840) and Bank of Madras (1843) to form Imperial Bank of India (1921) → nationalised as STATE BANK OF INDIA by SBI Act 1955. So SBI is the OLDEST surviving bank via Bank of Calcutta (1806). Bank of Hindustan (1770) was EARLIER but defunct by 1832. Allahabad Bank (1865) was India's first FULLY INDIAN-MANAGED joint-stock bank; it merged into Indian Bank in 2020. Punjab National Bank (1894) — first bank fully managed by Indians.

questions.stem: Bank nationalisation in India happened in two phases. Which year did the SECOND phase of bank nationalisation occur?
questions.explanation: FIRST phase: 19 July 1969 — Indira Gandhi nationalised 14 major private banks (those with deposits > ₹50 crore) via the Banking Companies Ordinance 1969. Banks included: Central BoI, BoI, PNB, BoB, UCO, Canara, Dena, Syndicate, Union, Allahabad, Indian, Indian Overseas, BoM, United Bank. SECOND phase: 15 April 1980 — 6 more private banks with deposits > ₹200 crore nationalised (Andhra Bank, Corporation, New Bank of India merged later with PNB, Oriental Bank, Punjab & Sind, Vijaya). Result: ~91% of banking system became public sector by 1980. Liberalisation in 1991 allowed new private banks (HDFC, ICICI, Axis etc.).

questions.stem: Which of the following is a regulator of NBFCs in India?
questions.explanation: NBFCs (Non-Banking Financial Companies) are regulated by RBI. Scale-Based Regulation (SBR) framework (effective Oct 2022) classifies NBFCs into 4 layers: (1) BASE Layer — smaller NBFCs (<₹1000 Cr assets) — minimum NOF ₹10 Cr by March 2027; (2) MIDDLE Layer; (3) UPPER Layer (identified by RBI as systemically important); (4) TOP Layer (reserved for extreme systemic risk cases). Types: AFC (Asset Finance), LC (Loan), ICC (Investment & Credit), IFC (Infrastructure Finance), MGC (Mortgage Guarantee), MFI (MicroFinance), HFC (Housing Finance — now regulated by RBI from NHB since 2019). SEBI regulates mutual funds/stock markets; IRDAI regulates insurance; PFRDA regulates pensions.
